t: Almost everything alive is too small to see. We only noticed any of it 350 years ago.
The overwhelming majority of living things are invisible without a lens, and nobody knew they existed until a Dutch draper ground his own and looked at pond water in the 1670s.
sub: For all of history before that, nobody knew.
Every explanation of disease before that date was constructed without the main cause of it.

question: What is the smallest thing you can see with just your eyes?
What is the resolution limit of the unaided human eye?
options: About the width of a hair — and bacteria are fifty times smaller
About the size of a bacterium
Anything, if you look closely enough
stages.outcome: About the width of a hair — and bacteria are fifty times smaller
note: Commit. A human hair is about 70 micrometres and a typical bacterium about 1 to 2.

stages.label: Zoom in
captions: 1 millimetre: a grain of sand. The smallest thing you can really examine.
70 micrometres: a human hair's width. About the limit of what you can see at all.
20 micrometres: one of your cells. Invisible without a microscope.
2 micrometres: a bacterium. Fifty of them across a hair.
100 nanometres: a virus. A hundred of those across a bacterium.
t: Go from something you can hold to something nobody saw for the whole of history.
Five steps from a sand grain to a virus. Note where the eye stops and where the light microscope stops.
after: Two whole levels of life below anything anyone could see.
The light microscope reaches bacteria and stops; viruses needed the electron microscope in the 1930s. Each instrument revealed a layer that had been there throughout.

t: Living things too small to see are called microbes, and there are more of them than everything else put together.
Microorganisms — bacteria, archaea, many fungi and protists — outnumber all visible life by an enormous margin, and always have.
Bacteria and archaea account for the majority of Earth's biological diversity and a substantial fraction of its biomass, much of it kilometres underground in rock.

Visible life is a thin and unrepresentative sample. Most of the genetic diversity on the planet is microbial, most metabolic strategies exist only in microbes, and the deep subsurface biosphere alone may hold a mass comparable to all surface life. Animals are the exception that happens to be doing the looking.
sub: They were doing everything for billions of years before anything bigger existed.
Life was exclusively microbial for roughly the first three billion years — most of its history.
Every major chemical trick — photosynthesis, nitrogen fixation, respiration — was invented by microbes and inherited by everything else.

Your mitochondria and a plant's chloroplasts are captured bacteria, retained as organelles. Complex life did not invent its own power supply; it acquired one, and the evidence is that both still carry their own genomes.

q: Why did nobody know about germs until 350 years ago?
Why was microbial life undiscovered for the whole of recorded history?
What made microbial life inaccessible before the 1670s?
options: They are far too small to see without a lens
There were fewer of them then
why: They were everywhere the whole time. Nobody could see them, and you cannot investigate something you have no way of detecting.

It was an instrument problem, not a curiosity problem. People had wondered about invisible causes of disease for centuries; what was missing was any way to look, and a good enough lens supplied it immediately.

The observation was gated entirely on optics, which is why the discovery arrives so suddenly and so completely once lens-making improves. It is a clean example of a whole domain of nature being inaccessible not for want of thought but for want of an instrument — and a reason to be careful about concluding that something does not exist.

t: Once people could see them, they worked out what was causing disease, and everything changed.

Germ theory follows directly from being able to see the germs, and it is arguably the single most consequential idea in the history of medicine — more lives saved by handwashing, clean water and sterile surgery than by any drug. All of it waited on a lens good enough to show that the cause was there at all.
